strategy:
1. Approach and rationale
Use exact-objective pairwise exchange search. From a feasible vector, choose two coordinates and transfer mass between them while preserving the sum, then globally minimize the original maximum-over-lags objective along that one-dimensional feasible segment. Combine this local search with deterministic transformations of the supplied construction, seeded starts, and a short basin-hopping phase that can temporarily accept worse local minima.

This is materially different from both the supplied parent and the previous strategy: it does not build an LP from lag linearizations, and it does not smooth the maximum or use SLSQP. Its line search uses the actual finite-lag quadratic expressions and their special curvature under a two-coordinate exchange. The mathematical facts supporting that line search are derived in section 2. The hypothesis is that exact nonsmooth coordinate searches and basin changes may reach a better construction than the parent’s trust-region steps; this is not a measured improvement or a guarantee. The method remains a nonconvex, restricted, finite-budget heuristic. Pair screening, finite starts, and local descent can miss improvements requiring coordinated movement in several coordinates, and no global-optimality claim is justified.

2. Mathematical specification
For runtime resolution n, let dx = 2/n, s = n/2, and require h in R^n with 0 ≤ h_i ≤ 1 and sum_i h_i = s. For integer lag d in {-(n-1), ..., n-1}, set a_d = max(d,0), b_d = max(-d,0), and m_d = n - |d|. Define

Q_d(h) = dx * sum_{r=0}^{m_d-1} h[a_d+r] * (1 - h[b_d+r]), and C(h) = max_d Q_d(h).

This is exactly np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode='full') * dx in increasing-lag order. It uses finite support: a lag has only n-|d| terms, indices never wrap, and both positive and negative lags are included. The mass condition gives dx * sum(h) = 1. There is no surrogate objective: every returned candidate is ranked by C(h) from the authoritative evaluator formula.

For a lag d, define its coordinate gradient g_d as follows. For each term with p=a_d+r and q=b_d+r, add dx*(1-h[q]) to g_d[p] and subtract dx*h[p] from g_d[q]. When d=0 both contributions apply to the same coordinate, giving dx*(1-2h[p]). For distinct coordinates i,j, use direction v=e_i-e_j and h(t)=h+t*v. Its feasible interval is

L = max(-h_i, h_j-1), U = min(1-h_i, h_j).

For every lag, Q_d(h(t)) = A_d*t^2 + B_d*t + D_d, where D_d=Q_d(h), B_d=g_d[i]-g_d[j], and A_d=-dx*sum_r v[a_d+r]*v[b_d+r]. For this two-coordinate direction, A_0=-2*dx; if r=|i-j|, A_r=A_-r=dx; all other nonzero-lag coefficients are zero. Thus every nonzero-lag polynomial is convex (linear or convex quadratic), while Q_0 is concave.

For n≥2, define G(t)=max over d≠0 of Q_d(h(t)) and H(t)=G(t)-Q_0(h(t)). G is convex. Each polynomial Q_d-Q_0 has strictly positive quadratic coefficient A_d+2*dx, so H is strongly convex. These facts make a global one-dimensional minimization of max(G,Q_0) possible without enumerating all pairwise polynomial intersections: minimize G and H on [L,U]; if min H≥0, G dominates everywhere. Otherwise H≤0 is a central interval, with at most one crossing on each side of its minimum. On the outside intervals G dominates and can be minimized as a convex function; on the central interval Q_0 dominates and, being concave, has its minimum at an interval endpoint. Golden-section minimization and bisection of the crossings therefore provide all required candidate locations up to stated numerical tolerance. Evaluate the polynomial maximum at these locations and retain t=0 as a candidate. Recompute the exact correlation score after constructing and repairing any selected vector.

3. Implementation procedure
3.1. Define top-level run(seed=42, **kwargs) and top-level helper functions only; do not use closures or lambdas. Use NumPy and the standard library; no solver is required. All checks, optimization, scoring, and fallback selection occur in the generated program. Read initial_h_values at runtime under exception handling; never redefine it or embed its entries.

Determine n as follows. If initial_h_values converts to a flattened float64 array with length from 1 through 999, preserve that length as n, regardless of whether its values later pass validation. Treat its values as a usable parent only if all are finite and lie in [-1e-8, 1+1e-8]. If there is no valid parent length, accept kwargs['n_points'] only if it converts to an integer-valued number in [1,999]; otherwise use n=47. Do not change a valid parent resolution. Convert seed to int, using 42 on failure, and create one seeded NumPy generator. If a parent is usable, clip only its tiny tolerated bound excursions and project it onto the feasible set to form a parent-derived fallback. If not, use the uniform vector as fallback. In all cases retain the fallback separately from search state.

3.2. Implement project_capped(z,n), returning either a jointly feasible float64 vector or failure. Reject wrong shape or nonfinite input; clip finite working values to [-1e12,1e12]. Find lambda by 80 bisection iterations on [min(z)-1, max(z)] for f(lambda)=sum(clip(z-lambda,0,1)); if f exceeds s=n/2, increase the lower endpoint, otherwise decrease the upper endpoint. Form h=clip(z-midpoint,0,1). Repair residual r=s-sum(h) in ascending coordinate order: for r>0 add min(r,1-h_i) at each coordinate; for r<0 subtract min(-r,h_i); update the residual after every change. Return failure if residual exceeds 1e-10*max(1,n), values are nonfinite, or any bound is violated. This is a joint capped-simplex feasibility operation, not successive clipping and rescaling. The uniform vector full(n,0.5) is always a valid fallback.

Implement is_feasible(h,n) to require shape (n,), finite entries, exact bounds 0≤h_i≤1, and absolute mass residual at most 1e-10*max(1,n). Implement exact_score(h,n) to return positive infinity on failed feasibility or nonfinite correlation, and otherwise return float(max(np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode='full') * (2.0/n))). This includes all 2n-1 finite-support lags and is the only score used for candidate acceptance, global-best storage, and return.

3.3. Implement lag_values(h,n) by the exact full np.correlate formula in section 2, returning a length-(2n-1) array with index k corresponding to d=k-(n-1). Implement lag_grad_entry(h,d,k,dx) from the slice rule in section 2: let p0=max(d,0), q0=max(-d,0), m=n-|d|; add dx*(1-h[q0+k-p0]) if k is in the p slice, and subtract dx*h[p0+k-q0] if k is in the q slice. These conditions both apply at d=0. Do not build a dense lag-by-coordinate gradient matrix.

3.4. Construct starts algorithmically and project each through project_capped. Add, in order, the fallback, its reversal, 1-fallback[::-1], the uniform vector, a contiguous block with floor(n/2) leading ones and (for odd n) one following 0.5, an alternating zero/one vector, a seeded balanced binary pattern, fallback plus Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.08, fallback plus Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.20, and a seeded uniform-random vector. A balanced binary pattern has n/2 ones if n is even; if n is odd it has floor(n/2) ones, one 0.5 at a seeded random position, and zeros elsewhere. Generate it by a seeded permutation, not a stored pattern. Deduplicate projected starts when their maximum coordinate difference is below 1e-8. If fewer than the configured number remain, try additional seeded balanced patterns and projected Gaussian perturbations, stopping after at most four times the requested count in attempts. Score every retained start exactly and order starts from lower to higher score before local search.

3.5. Implement pair screening at each local-search iteration. Use the eight largest lag values as the screening set (or all lags if fewer); screening only ranks directions and never replaces the exact line search. Compute their gradients with lag_grad_entry. For an unordered pair i<j, let b_d=g_d[i]-g_d[j]. The largest screened right-direction slope is max_d b_d and the largest left-direction slope is max_d(-b_d). Its merit is the smaller of the slopes for directions that have nonzero feasible room, where L=max(-h_i,h_j-1) and U=min(1-h_i,h_j). Lower merit is tried first. For n≤128 enumerate all unordered pairs with NumPy upper-triangle indices. For n>128 use at most min(3000,6*n) seeded sampled unordered pairs, and add pairs connecting the lowest and highest gradient coordinates for each screened lag (use at most eight coordinates at each extreme). Rank the resulting pairs by merit, take the configured number of best, and add the configured number of distinct seeded random pairs. Skip pairs with U-L≤1e-12. If no pair remains, end the local descent.

3.6. Implement pair_line_min(h,q,i,j,n) for the global one-dimensional line search. Set dx=2/n, D=q, B_d=lag_grad_entry(h,d,i,dx)-lag_grad_entry(h,d,j,dx), and initialize A to zero. Set A at the zero-lag index n-1 to -2*dx and at indices n-1±|i-j| to dx. Compute L and U from section 2. If coefficients or interval are invalid, return failure. Implement top-level helpers that evaluate P_d(t)=A_d*t^2+B_d*t+D_d, G(t)=max of P_d over nonzero lags, and H(t)=G(t)-P_0(t). Implement golden-section minimization for G and H on any closed interval using 52 iterations, checking finite values and comparing interval endpoints and the final interior points. Implement root bisection for H using 52 iterations on a bracket whose endpoint values have opposite signs.

Let tG and tH be the golden-section minimizers on [L,U]. Start the line-search candidate list with L, U, clip(0,L,U), tG, and tH. If H(tH)≥0, G dominates throughout and these candidates include its minimizer. If H(tH)<0, find a left root between L and tH only when H(L)>0, and a right root between tH and U only when H(U)>0. Add each root. On each resulting outer interval where H≥0, add a golden-section minimizer of G restricted to that interval. The remaining central interval has H≤0, so Q_0 dominates there and its concavity means its minimum is at one of the already included central endpoints. Evaluate max_d P_d(t) at every finite candidate, choose the lowest value, and on numerical ties prefer the t with smaller absolute magnitude. This solves the original max along the pair direction, not a smoothed approximation. For n=1 there are no pairs and this helper is not called.

3.7. Implement local_descent(start,n,rng,settings). Project and validate start; initialize current score with exact_score. For at most the configured move limit, recompute the exact lag array, screen pairs as specified, and call pair_line_min for each selected pair. For every successful t, form a trial by adding t to h_i and subtracting t from h_j, then pass it through project_capped to remove floating-point mass error. Reject failed projections and infeasible vectors; compute exact_score for every remaining trial. Select the trial with the lowest exact score. Accept it only if it improves the current score by more than 1e-12 and changes some coordinate by at least 1e-10. Otherwise stop this descent. The accepted sequence is nonincreasing in the exact objective. Return its feasible terminal vector and recomputed exact score. A failed pair calculation skips only that pair; an exception or invalid trial must not discard the current feasible vector.

Initialize global_best to fallback and global_score to its exact score. Score every start and update the global best on a strict improvement greater than 1e-12. Run local_descent from each retained start, updating the global best whenever its returned score improves it. Keep fallback untouched throughout.

3.8. Add a short basin-hopping phase after the multistart descents. Initialize walker to global_best and walker_score to global_score. For each configured hop, perturb walker by seeded independent Gaussian noise, project, and run local_descent with the shorter hop move limit. Use the cyclic per-coordinate noise standard deviations 0.04, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, multiplied by clip(sqrt(47/n),0.5,1.5). Skip failed proposals. Update global_best only for an exact-score improvement greater than 1e-12. Let delta=proposal_score-walker_score and T=0.0015*(0.25+0.75*(1-hop_index/number_of_hops)). Accept the proposal as the new walker if delta≤1e-12; otherwise accept with probability exp(-min(700,delta/T)) using the seeded generator. On rejection retain the previous walker. This permits basin changes without risking the separately stored global best or fallback.

3.9. Before return, project global_best once, validate it, and recompute its exact score. If this fails, use fallback. If its score is worse than fallback_score by more than 1e-12, use fallback. Validate and score the selected vector again. If any remaining recovery step fails, use full(n,0.5) and compute its score with the same exact scorer. Return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), with h_values a length-n float64 NumPy array, c5_bound a Python float, and n_points an integer.

4. Search choices and useful variations
Use these defaults without preliminary tuning: for n≤64 retain up to 10 distinct starts, allow 24 accepted local moves per full descent, screen 5 pairs and add 3 random pairs per move, and perform 6 basin hops with 10 local moves each. For 65≤n≤128 use 7 starts, 16 full moves, 5 screened plus 2 random pairs, and 4 hops with 7 moves. For 129≤n≤256 use 4 starts, 8 full moves, 4 screened plus 2 random pairs, and 3 hops with 4 moves. For n>256 use 3 starts, 5 full moves, 3 screened plus 1 random pair, and 2 hops with 3 moves. Keep the eight-lag screening set and 52 scalar iterations by default.

Practical variations within this same method are 4-12 screening lags, 3-8 screened pairs, 1-4 random pairs, 40-64 golden/bisection iterations, and modestly more starts or hops for n≤64. Larger budgets increase exact correlation evaluations, so decrease them as n grows. The active-lag gradient and Metropolis choices are search heuristics only; exact finite-lag score, full lag range, capped-simplex feasibility, and fallback preservation are correctness requirements. Any result-dependent Metropolis acceptance must execute inside run. No parameter choice promises the target bound or a global optimum.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use
Use float64 throughout. The exact score and lag vector use O(n) output memory and O(n^2) work for np.correlate. Pair line coefficients and active gradients use O(n) memory. Enumerating all pairs is limited to n≤128; above that, pair candidates are sampled and capped, so no large dense pair-by-lag or lag-by-coordinate matrix is formed. The largest gradient array is at most eight by n. Search counts decrease with n, and the execution uses one CPU. This is especially small at the supplied 47-point resolution; do not claim measured runtime.

The capped-simplex projection checks finiteness, clips extreme finite working values, uses bounded bisection, and corrects mass only within available capacity. Exact lag evaluation must reject nonfinite values. The scalar searches use bounded intervals, fixed iteration limits, and finite-value checks; if a line calculation fails, retain the current feasible point. Do not divide by a vector norm or by a potentially zero quantity. Clamp the Metropolis exponent as specified. Seed all random generation. Stop each local descent on its move limit, no strict exact-score improvement, or a negligible step; stop basin hopping after its fixed count. There is no stationarity or global-convergence guarantee. Maintain the uniform fallback and any usable parent-derived fallback even if every search operation fails.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract
The generated program must define top-level run(seed=42, **kwargs), use initial_h_values only as an optional supplied runtime input, and perform all optimization and objective calculations in program code. Check runtime length, finiteness, bounds, mass, projection success, and exact score before accepting any candidate. Preserve a feasible parent-derived fallback whenever a parent with valid length and usable values exists, and preserve the uniform fallback in all cases. Candidate acceptance and global-best selection use the exact full linear correlation score, never line-search polynomial or screening merit alone. On any invalid result or unexpected search failure, recover to the validated fallback and finally to full(n,0.5). Return the specified three-tuple with a recomputed exact C5 bound, with no filesystem or network I/O.
